I think the main cause of shit-posting and terrible comment chains is the result of a massive user base. If you're a member of any smaller subs, you'll notice that the content there is generally of a higher quality or at least evident that the submitter put more time and effort into it. The larger the sub, the higher probability more people will see the content and comment on it. There is a rush to be the first person to make a comment, otherwise the chances are good you will go unnoticed among the other hundreds of comments. It's quick and easy to say "I did nazi that coming" but it takes time and effort to provide a thoughtful comment. Sometimes we still see the more thought out comments rise to the top, but in my opinion it happens less and less as the size of a site/sub increases.

I think what Voat has done as far as the ccp limits and restrictions is a good start as it discourages lurkers from mass upvoting/downvoting and encourages contribution. Before the AMAgeddon or whatever they're calling it, users here generally only used the downvote for posts or comments that did not contribute to the subverse. I think having stricter limits on the user's daily allowable upvotes could be a possible solution as it would force users to be more conservative with their votes. I also think this would anger many people and would not receive a favorable reaction.

The large userbase has another effect on the type of posts and at least perceived quality. While in the beginning Reddit was the home to a homogeneous community, it through expansion saw more niche subreddits pop up to fulfill the desires different groups of users had. After a while all of these identity subreddits such as SRS or TRP became big enough to become semi-autarkical communities, fighting against each other and using the downvote button to punish those who dissented with them.

The problem is that all these metaphorical gangs had to share common grounds in prison in non-identity subreddits such /r/askreddit or /r/worldnews where the increase in heterogeneity caused the distance between the hivemind and any random user to grow. Often it was the case in for example AskReddit threads that people would become mad for the theme or direction that the comments had (e.g. puns but in a broader sense ideology).

For the same reason Reddit would have been much shittier if it merged with Tumblr, Voat has become shittier because it merged with a large group of a different type of Redditors than the type of Redditors who came before.
Don't you think it's a little premature to claim that Voat has become shittier because a lot of different types of people came here than before?

As /u/Cyclonetoo stated it is because of attention, which to me doesn't really provide the full explanatory power of the main cause - the question why they get this attention still remains. In the case of /v/askvoat shitposts get more attention because they are accessible and easy to answer for many people. The question: 'How would the Stoics adopt their philosophy to fit modern science?' would only be accessible for a few whereas the question: 'what is your favourite movie?' will generate a ton of responses. People either upvote the latter post because that will increase the likelihood of their answer getting points as well, or they genuinely think it is an interesting question and their answer original.

Both these explanations would very roughly come down to shitposting getting more attention because of shit-for-brain people upvoting them. The solution to this would be to make this site harder to find or tougher moderation.
